state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Why do you think Tom believes that cutting all the plants in half wouldn't change the range? Can you think of a scenario where changing all the values by the same proportion would actually change the range?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, I think Tom means like if you cut them all in half, the difference between the biggest and smallest would still be the same... but now I'm confused because if 42 becomes 21 and 13 becomes 6.5, isn't 21 minus 6.5 different from 42 minus 13? So maybe the range does change when you multiply?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track with your thinking. Can you think of a different example where changing all the values by the same proportion would change the range? How might that apply to the situation with the plant heights?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh wait, I think I see it now - when you multiply by half, like 42 minus 13 is 29, but 21 minus 6.5 is only 14.5, so the range actually does get smaller! So Tom is wrong too? But then what about Katie's thing with adding 3 cm - does that change the range or not?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the specific misconception about proportional changes through guided questioning that leads the student to discover that multiplication changes range while addition doesn't, though the dialogue ends before fully resolving Katie's case.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking, never provides direct answers, and successfully uses the student's own reasoning to expose the flaw in their initial conclusion about Tom being correct.
